title: Exchanging self and other
hookLine: Shantideva: put yourself in another's place, completely

lines: THE HAND GOES TO THE FOOT.
cards: A stubbed toe. The hand goes straight down to it. Nobody tells the hand to, and it never stops to ask what the foot has done for it lately.
It just goes, because hand and foot belong to one body.
In the masterpiece the lazy monk recited, the guide to the bodhisattva's way of life, a chapter on meditation takes that ordinary reflex and pushes it as far as it will go.
What if the line around the body were drawn somewhere else?

teach.b: Shantideva builds it in steps. I want to be happy and I don't want to suffer. So does everyone else, in exactly the same way.

If that's true, he asks, what makes my pain the one worth guarding? Only habit. He uses the picture of the body: the hand protects the foot as part of itself, and so beings can be cared for as parts of one life.
Put yourself where the other person stands, and look back.
In one passage he has the practitioner take the place of someone worse off, then an equal, then someone better off, and look back at their old self from each seat, calling that old self he.
From the other side of the table, my own pride looks very different. Why bother?
Shantideva is blunt: the misery in the world comes from wanting happiness only for oneself, and the joy in the world comes from wishing others well.
He calls this exchange a supreme secret, a practice for those who want to protect themselves and others quickly. And what it isn't.
It isn't erasing yourself, or pretending you have no needs.
The practitioner still eats and sleeps. It's a shift of where the center sits, practiced on purpose, the way a musician practices scales. Tibetan teachers later built whole trainings on this chapter.
In these verses his tone is plain and urgent, with nothing sentimental in it.

how: In Tibetan Buddhism, exchanging self and other is taught from the eighth chapter of Shantideva's Bodhicaryavatara, and it underlies mind-training practices in which practitioners imagine taking on others' suffering and giving away their own happiness.

o: swapping gifts to keep a friendship even
trading old vows for new ones each year
trading places: standing where another stands

games.q: exchanging self and other: tap the pairs.

s: exchanging self and other means ignoring your own needs
the practitioner still eats and sleeps. it moves where the center sits.
Shantideva grounds it in everyone wanting happiness
the same wish in everyone is his starting point.
the practice comes from the meditation chapter of his guide
it's taught in the chapter on meditation in the guide to the bodhisattva's way.

games.q: you're Shantideva's student. your hand rushes to a hurt foot without thinking. what do you take from it?
o: the body looks after itself, so let others look after themselves.
the line around 'mine' can be drawn wider.
reflexes are just reflexes; ignore them.
games.why: Shantideva uses the body's care for its own parts as a picture of caring for beings as parts of one life.

practice: Bring to mind one person you saw yesterday, anyone at all, and sit where they sat: their chair, their morning, their tiredness, what they were hoping for.
From there, look across at yourself without judging what you see, then come home to your own breath.

wordCard.voice: Exchange. Shantideva's practice of standing where another stands and wanting their good as if it were your own, which he calls a supreme secret. Today's word.

orig.note: Sanskrit for exchanging self and other: para, other; atma, self; parivartana, turning around.

carryVoice: Your line: exchange self and other. The hand never asks what the foot has done for it. Day nine hundred sixty-seven.
